structure.title: Dedication, introduction and chapters I–III · Put education on the public agenda
structure.text: Wollstonecraft addresses a French statesman before she addresses the people who teach girls how to please. The order matters. A country deciding how to educate its citizens has already made a political decision if half the population is trained principally for dependence.

structure.title: Chapters IV–VIII · Who taught the admired woman her part?
structure.text: Conduct writers, philosophers and polite society offer competing lessons in a remarkably similar femininity. Wollstonecraft follows early associations into adult habits and asks what becomes of moral judgment when an impeccable reputation is more valuable to a woman than honest conduct.

structure.title: Chapters IX–XIII · Rebuild the household and the school
structure.text: Rank, parental affection and children's obligations widen the case beyond courtship. Proposals for national education give her criticism a practical test. What kind of school could prepare children who must later live together as reasoning adults?

people.name: Rousseau
people.text: His plan for educating a girl to suit a man gives Wollstonecraft a precise adversary. She asks how qualities trained through rewards and constraints could then be cited as evidence of a naturally subordinate character.

people.name: The woman taught to please
people.role: A successful pupil of a damaging system
people.text: Dependence makes the ability to read another person's wishes economically useful. Wollstonecraft's anger at manipulation and vanity becomes more intelligible when one asks what independent means of action a woman has actually been allowed to acquire.

context.title: Virtue has to be a human capacity
context.text: Wollstonecraft treats reason and moral accountability as claims made on both sexes. Praising women for a special innocence can remove the very capacity for independent judgment that would make an action worthy of praise.

notice.why: Soldiers trained for display and obedience can acquire traits conventionally described as feminine. The comparison gives Wollstonecraft something close to a control case for an argument about the effects of education.

notice.text: Notice the price paid for being called modest.
notice.why: Reputation can be lost through appearances that say little about conduct. The social power of the accusation then rewards secrecy and calculation, traits the same society will later deplore in women.

opening: Girls are trained to be pleasing, dependent, and preoccupied with appearance. Then men cite those qualities as evidence that women are naturally unfit for independence. Mary Wollstonecraft attacks the arrangement at its source: an education designed to make obedience attractive and reason unnecessary. Her argument makes demands on women as well as men, insisting that dignity involves developing judgment and accepting responsibility. The force of this early feminist work comes from refusing the compliments that help keep a person permanently in someone else's care.
